questions.q: How does AWS describe the two halves of the shared responsibility model?
options: Security of the cloud (the provider's job) versus security in the cloud (the customer's job)
Security during business hours versus security after hours
Security for free-tier accounts versus security for paid accounts
Security for the United States region versus security for all other regions
questions.explain: AWS's own terminology splits responsibility into security OF the cloud (physical infrastructure, the provider's job) and security IN the cloud (data, identity, configuration — the customer's job).

questions.q: Who is responsible for a publicly exposed storage bucket that leaks sensitive data?
options: The customer, always — regardless of which service tier they're using
The cloud provider, since they built the storage service
Responsibility is split 50/50 between customer and provider automatically
Nobody — it's considered an unavoidable risk of using cloud storage
questions.explain: Per the shared responsibility model, access configuration is always the customer's responsibility. A misconfigured bucket permission is a customer-side failure, even though the provider built and secured the underlying storage service.

questions.q: What changes as you move from IaaS to PaaS to SaaS?
options: The provider takes on more of the infrastructure and platform management, but the customer still owns access and classification decisions
The customer takes on progressively more responsibility at each step
Data governance responsibility shifts entirely to the provider once you reach SaaS
Nothing changes — the responsibility split is identical at every service tier
questions.explain: The provider's share of the stack grows (OS patching, database engine management, and more), but the lesson stresses that the customer's data-governance responsibilities — classification and access control — barely shrink at all, even at the SaaS tier.

questions.q: What is the one responsibility that never transfers to the cloud provider, at any service tier?
options: Deciding which data is sensitive and who should be allowed to access it
Securing the physical data center
Patching the hypervisor
Maintaining the network backbone between regions
questions.explain: The provider can supply tools like encryption-by-default and strong IAM primitives, but it cannot decide for the customer what counts as sensitive data or who should see it — those are governance decisions that always stay with the customer.

questions.q: Why does the lesson call "we moved to the cloud, so it's secure now" a dangerous sentence?
options: Because most cloud data breaches trace back to a customer-side misconfiguration, not a provider failure
Because cloud providers have historically had worse security track records than on-premises data centers
Because moving to the cloud actually increases the provider's share of responsibility to 100%
Because cloud providers explicitly disclaim all responsibility for any part of the stack
questions.explain: The lesson points out that major cloud breaches have overwhelmingly been traced to misconfigurations on the customer's side of the responsibility line — overly permissive IAM policies, public buckets, unencrypted databases — not provider failures.
